entities.title: Measure capability in task horizon, not single-turn accuracy
entities.text: Progress in any multi-step system is most honestly tracked by the duration and coherence of work it can complete unaided, not by accuracy on isolated atomic problems. Pick-one-question benchmarks systematically under-represent the failure modes that actually matter when work chains across hours or days.

entities.title: Treat specialisation as a first-class competitive strategy
entities.text: A narrow, deeply-scaffolded system with domain-specific tools and evaluators can outperform a larger generic system on that domain. Betting on 'one universal model' underweights the leverage of environment, tool, and eval design that only makes sense inside a specific workflow.

entities.title: Long-horizon RL is a categorically different problem from single-turn RL
entities.text: Once episodes contain many state-changing actions, tool calls, and delayed rewards, the naive RLVR loop (prompt â†’ answer â†’ verifier) no longer applies. Data collection, latency, environment stability, observability, and verifier design move from implementation detail to dominant constraints.

entities.title: Credit assignment is the central bottleneck in long trajectories
entities.text: When success or failure follows many interacting steps, attributing which action mattered is the hard problem. Dense step-level labels do not scale, so trajectory logs, inspectable observations, and evals that separate outcome quality from process quality are prerequisites for learnable feedback.

entities.title: Environments are training infrastructure, not context
entities.text: A realistic, stable, hard-to-game environment with genuine state and dynamics is a capital asset. If the environment is slow, brittle, or trivially exploitable, no amount of algorithmic work recovers the lost signal â€” environment quality caps what any training loop can achieve.

entities.title: Choose frameworks per use-case; a universal stack is not coming
entities.text: The tooling landscape is fragmented for structural reasons â€” local vs distributed scale, model size, hardware mix, and objective all pull in different directions. Waiting for one canonical framework is a stall; picking the one that fits the specific objective beats chasing generality.

entities.title: Treat benchmarks as perishable and adversarial, not scoreboards
entities.text: Public benchmarks saturate, get overfit to, and stop discriminating. The durable value of a benchmark is in surfacing what a system still cannot do, so they must be continuously rebuilt to be harder, more realistic, and harder to reward-hack.

entities.title: Scaffolding can deliver capability gains before any new training
entities.text: Test-time compute, decomposition, self-aggregation, retrieval, and orchestration all raise effective performance of a fixed model. Treating scaffold as a side concern and training as the lever leaves most of the available capability on the table.

entities.title: Ratchet evaluation targets toward work nobody has done before
entities.text: A useful progression for eval design: exam-style â†’ multi-day human work â†’ multi-year team work â†’ verifiable novel work. Pushing targets rightward is what keeps evals discriminative and forces the infrastructure needed to train against the next capability tier.

entities.title: Internal, real-task evals are the durable strategic asset
entities.text: Generic public benchmarks are a commodity and don't transfer to the task a team actually cares about. Internal evals grounded in real work, designed adversarially against reward hacking, are what let a team detect real progress and direct training effort.
